title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
description: Find the kth largest value using a bounded min-heap, and compare it with sorting and quickselect.

data.text: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k`th largest element. Note that this is the `k`th largest in sorted order, not the `k`th distinct element.
Sort descending and index `k - 1`. Simple, but it does far more work than necessary — you only need one element, not a total order.

data.title: Sort O(n log n)

data.text: Keep a min-heap containing at most `k` elements — the largest `k` seen so far. When a new value arrives and the heap is full, push it and then pop the smallest. The root is always the smallest of the top `k`, which is exactly the answer at the end.

data.title: Min-Heap of size k — O(n log k)
data.content: The heap is capped at k, so it beats a full sort when k is small.

data.title: Why a min-heap for the kth largest?
data.text: The heap stores the top k. The *weakest* member of that group is the smallest, which sits at the root of a min-heap — so the root is precisely the cutoff value you want. Using a max-heap would require draining k elements at the end instead.

data.title: PriorityQueue in .NET
data.text: `System.Collections.Generic.PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority>` orders by priority, smallest first, and is a min-heap. For a max-heap, negate the priority or pass a custom comparer.
Partition around a pivot as in quicksort, but recurse into only the side that contains the target index. Average O(n), worst case O(n²) with bad pivot choices.

data.title: Quickselect — average O(n)
data.content: Discard half the array on each partition.

data.caption: The min-heap never holds more than k elements; its root is the current kth largest value.

cards.title: Full sort
cons: O(n log n) even for small k

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: Prefer the heap when k is small relative to n, when the data arrives as a stream, or when you also need the top k values. Prefer quickselect when k is around n/2 and you want the average-case linear guarantee.
